title: NZ Health Information Privacy Code disclosure
body: This clinic may use governed AI tools to support clinical queries and documentation. Identifying details should be protected before information is processed, and a record of the session is kept for safety and audit.

title: Privacy and clinical AI disclosure
body: This clinic may use governed AI tools to support clinical queries and documentation. Identifying details should be protected before information is processed, and a record of the session is kept for safety and audit.

title: AI use in your consultation
body: This clinic uses AI tools to help clinicians answer clinical questions and prepare documentation. Before information is sent for AI processing, identifying details should be removed or transformed. A session record is kept for privacy and safety.

title: Offshore processing notice
body: Some governed AI processing for this session may occur outside New Zealand. This clinic keeps an audit record of the processing path and applies controls before information is sent offshore.

title: AI-assisted care disclosure
body: This provider may use governed AI to support clinical queries and documentation. Patient information should be handled under the Privacy Act and Australian Privacy Principles, with controls applied before any external processing.

title: AI-assisted care disclosure
body: This provider may use governed AI to support clinical queries and documentation. Patient information should be handled under the Privacy Act and Australian Privacy Principles, with controls applied before any external processing.

title: Clinician responsibility for AI use
body: AI outputs are advisory only and remain subject to clinician judgement. This session uses governance controls so the provider can review what was asked, what protections were active, and what was recorded.

title: Aged care resident and guardian disclosure
body: This aged care service may use governed AI support under staff supervision. Proxy or guardian consent workflows, patient capacity concerns, and reportable safety issues must be handled under the clinic or facility's approved governance process.

title: HIPAA-aligned AI disclosure
body: This provider may use governed AI support during care delivery. Protected health information should be handled through approved paths with de-identification or minimum necessary controls and audit logging.

title: HIPAA-aligned AI disclosure

title: California AI communication disclosure

title: Texas AI disclosure

title: UK AI and privacy disclosure
body: This provider may use governed AI support under UK data protection expectations. Session-level controls and audit records are maintained for accountability.

title: EU high-risk AI session disclosure
body: This healthcare session may use governed AI support in a regulated context. The clinic records consent, model controls, and audit evidence for the session.

title: Child protection reporting (NSW)
body: Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 (NSW) ss 23, 27 and 154. Persons who deliver health care to children in their professional work, and registered psychologists, must report reasonable grounds to suspect that a child is at risk of significant harm (physical or sexual abuse, psychological harm, neglect, exposure to domestic violence) to the Secretary as soon as practicable. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: NSW: health care workers and registered psychologists must report reasonable grounds to suspect risk of significant harm (physical, sexual, psychological, neglect, exposure to domestic violence) to the Secretary (Child Protection Helpline).

title: Child protection reporting (VIC)
body: Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 (Vic) ss 182, 184 and 162(1)(c)-(d). Registered medical practitioners, nurses, midwives and registered psychologists must report a belief on reasonable grounds that a child needs protection because of significant harm from physical injury or sexual abuse and the parents have not protected or are unlikely to protect the child, to the Secretary as soon as practicable. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: Victoria: medical practitioners, nurses, midwives and registered psychologists must report reasonable belief of significant harm from physical injury or sexual abuse where parents are not protecting the child (to the Secretary, Child Protection).

title: Child protection reporting (QLD)
body: Child Protection Act 1999 (Qld) s 13E. Doctors and registered nurses must report a reasonable suspicion that a child has suffered, is suffering or is at unacceptable risk of suffering significant harm caused by physical or sexual abuse and may not have a parent able and willing to protect them. Psychologists are not mandated reporters under s 13E but may report. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: Queensland: doctors and registered nurses must report reasonable suspicion of significant harm from physical or sexual abuse with no parent able and willing to protect; psychologists may report but are not mandated under s 13E.

title: Child protection reporting (WA)
body: Children and Community Services Act 2004 (WA) ss 124A and 124B. Psychologists, doctors, nurses, midwives, teachers, school counsellors and others must report a belief on reasonable grounds formed in the course of their work that a child has been the subject of sexual abuse. The duty is limited to sexual abuse; other concerns are reported under service policy. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: Western Australia: psychologists, doctors, nurses, midwives and school counsellors must report reasonable belief of child sexual abuse (the statutory duty covers sexual abuse only) to the Department CEO.

title: Child protection reporting (SA)
body: Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 (SA) ss 17, 18, 30 and 31. Prescribed health practitioners including medical practitioners, nurses and psychologists, and employees of organisations providing health or welfare services to children, must report a suspicion on reasonable grounds that a child is, or may be, at risk (harm of a kind against which children are ordinarily protected, including sexual, physical, mental or emotional abuse or neglect) through the Child Abuse Report Line as soon as reasonably practicable. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: South Australia: health practitioners including psychologists must report reasonable suspicion that a child is or may be at risk (sexual, physical, mental or emotional abuse, neglect) via the Child Abuse Report Line.

title: Child protection reporting (TAS)
body: Children, Young Persons and Their Families Act 1997 (Tas) ss 3, 4 and 14. Medical practitioners, nurses, psychologists and others must report a belief or suspicion on reasonable grounds that a child has been or is being abused or neglected, or is affected by family violence, or is likely to be killed, abused or neglected by a person they live with, to the Secretary or a Community-Based Intake Service. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: Tasmania: medical practitioners, nurses and psychologists must report reasonable belief or suspicion of abuse, neglect or a child affected by family violence to the Secretary or a Community-Based Intake Service.

title: Child protection reporting (ACT)
body: Children and Young People Act 2008 (ACT) s 356. Doctors, nurses, midwives, psychologists, teachers and persons employed to counsel children at a school must report a belief on reasonable grounds, arising from their work, that a child has experienced or is experiencing sexual abuse or non-accidental physical injury, to the Director-General as soon as practicable. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: ACT: doctors, nurses, psychologists and school counsellors must report reasonable belief of sexual abuse or non-accidental physical injury to the Director-General (Child and Youth Protection Services).

title: Child protection reporting (NT)
body: Care and Protection of Children Act 2007 (NT) ss 15, 16 and 26. Any person must report a belief on reasonable grounds that a child has suffered or is likely to suffer harm or exploitation, and health practitioners must additionally report a reasonable belief that a child aged 14 or 15 has been or is likely to be the victim of a sexual offence where the age gap exceeds two years, to the CEO or a police officer. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: Northern Territory: any person must report reasonable belief that a child has suffered or is likely to suffer harm or exploitation; health practitioners also report sexual offences against 14 to 15 year olds (to the CEO or police).

title: Mental Health Act 2007 (NSW): boundaries for AI assistance
body: Compulsory assessment, detention, treatment orders and capacity determinations in this state are made under the Mental Health Act 2007 (NSW) by authorised clinicians and tribunals. This AI tool does not make or support those determinations, does not assess risk level, and its output is advisory and clinician-reviewed. Where a session shows language consistent with imminent danger, the clinician follows the service's crisis and escalation procedure; the tool records the signal, the acknowledgement and the follow-up.
summary: Mental Health Act 2007 (NSW): compulsory assessment, treatment and capacity decisions are made by authorised clinicians under the Act; this AI tool is advisory, does not assess risk level, and records signals, acknowledgement and follow-up only.

Identifying details are removed or replaced before AI processing, the AI tool retains no clinical content, and the signed session record contains hashes, identifiers and roles only.
summary: Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 (NSW) applies to health information in this state; identifying details are removed before AI processing and the session record holds hashes, identifiers and roles only.

title: Automated decision-making transparency (Privacy Act 1988, from 10 December 2026)
body: From 10 December 2026 an APP entity's privacy policy must describe the kinds of personal information used in, and the kinds of decisions made by, computer programs that make or substantially assist decisions which significantly affect an individual, including decisions about access to health services. Outputs of this AI tool are advisory, reviewed and signed off by a clinician, and never decide access to care; the service's privacy policy should say so.
summary: Privacy Act ADM transparency (from 10 December 2026): the privacy policy must describe automated decisions that significantly affect people; this tool is advisory and clinician-reviewed and never decides access to care.

title: Mental Health Act 2026 transition
body: The Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 remains in force until the Mental Health Act 2026 (Royal Assent 9 July 2026) commences on 1 July 2028. Compulsory assessment and treatment decisions are made by authorised clinicians under the applicable Act. This AI tool does not make or support those decisions, does not assess risk level, and records signals, acknowledgement and follow-up only.
summary: NZ: the MH(CAT) Act 1992 applies until the Mental Health Act 2026 commences on 1 July 2028; compulsory decisions are the clinician's under the Act; this tool is advisory and records signals, acknowledgement and follow-up.

title: Reporting concerns about a child (Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 s 15)
body: Under section 15 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 any person who believes a child or young person has been, or is likely to be, harmed, ill-treated, abused, neglected or deprived may report the matter to Oranga Tamariki or the Police. Reporting is permissive, not mandatory, and section 16 protects good-faith reporters. This AI tool records the signal, requires clinician acknowledgement and follow-up, and does not make a report or decide whether a legal duty applies. Clinicians follow their service's child protection procedure.
summary: NZ: reporting a concern about a child to Oranga Tamariki or the Police under s 15 is permissive, not mandatory; this tool records the signal and obliges acknowledgement and follow-up; it does not report.

title: Medical Council of New Zealand: AI in patient care (March 2026)
body: The Medical Council's guidance (approved 17 February 2026, published 10 March 2026) requires that doctors remain responsible for all clinical decisions and check AI output before using it (paras 1-4); document AI use in the patient's notes and their reasoning when not following an AI recommendation (para 5); ensure patients know when AI is used, with explicit information for high-risk AI (paras 7-8); obtain and always document informed consent when AI records the consultation, when personal details leave the primary record, or when AI plays a significant role in care (paras 9-10); and use AI only with appropriate oversight and without sharing identifiable information outside the care setting (paras 11-13). The session record captures the disclosure and consent state the clinician declares.
summary: MCNZ AI guidance (March 2026): document AI use in the notes, tell patients AI is used (explicitly for high-risk AI), obtain and always record informed consent when AI records the consultation or plays a significant role, and keep identifiable data inside the care setting.

title: Health New Zealand AI Pre-Implementation Evaluation Framework
body: Health New Zealand's Board endorsed the AI Pre-Implementation Evaluation Framework in July 2026 as the methodology the National AI and Algorithm Expert Advisory Group uses to assess whether an AI tool is safe, secure, ethical and equitable for patients, whanau, staff and the health system before implementation. This tool's signed session records are offered as evidence for that evaluation and for ongoing monitoring; they do not replace it.
summary: Health NZ AI Pre-Implementation Evaluation Framework (July 2026): tools are assessed as safe, secure, ethical and equitable before implementation; signed session records are evidence for that evaluation, not a substitute.
